newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish court convicts two for costly booze imports.
newsitem.headline: Polish court convicts two for costly booze imports.

text.p: Poland's State Tribunal convicted two former ministers on Wednesday over the so-called Schnapsgate affair of 1989-90, when a flood of nearly duty-free alcohol imports cost the treasury vast sums of money.

In its first verdict since it was formed in 1982 to try high officials, the tribunal cleared three other ministers accused of responsibility for letting cheap alcohol pour into Poland as it moved from communism to a market economy.

PAP news agency said the tribunal convicted Dominik Jastrzebski, who was Foreign Economic Relations Minister in the last communist government, and the former chairman of the Central Customs Office (GUC) Jerzy Cwiek, of infringing laws governing their departments and encouraging sobriety.
The two were disqualified from standing for election or holding office for five years, the agency said.

The court cleared the ex-ministers of the home market Aleksander Mackiewicz, of finance Andrzej Wroblewski and of the interior Czeslaw Kiszczak, who had been in the last communist cabinet or in the first democratic government after 1989.
"The tribunal found guilty those who by their actions caused the deluge and cleared those who did not find adequate means to halt it," leading judge Anna Bogucka-Skowronska was quoted as saying.
In December 1988 Jastrzebski scrapped a law which had obliged people importing alcohol for personal use rather than trade to get special concessions. He also set minimal duties for such imports.

According to the official watchdog body, the Supreme Auditing Chamber (NIK), from early 1989 to mid-1990 an estimated 30 million litres of liquor streamed across Poland's borders causing unknown millions of dollars of lost revenue at a time when the state revenues were extremely tight.

The ministers accused in the case argued that the episode stemmed from well-intentioned efforts to liberalise the former rigid communist-era restraints on trade, while prosecutors said they were guilty of negligence.
Cwiek said he would appeal against the verdict, while Jastrzebski said he had yet to decide, PAP reported.

Tribunal judge Bogucka-Skowronska said the extent of the financial losses was impossible to determine but that the affair had caused great social harm by allowing fortunes to be made when many people were very hard up, the agency said.

She said it hurt agriculture by cutting demand for potatoes used in making vodka and caused an outflow of foreign currency used in buying the liquor, as well as hitting profits of the Polish state distiller Polmos.
